tagline: Oil exploration and mountain mail shaped a drive through red-rock country
intro: Red Gulch/Alkali is a National Back Country Byway through the Bighorn foothills, with 32 miles of improved gravel and dirt. The Bureau of Land Management highlights its rugged canyons and wind-carved hoodoos. Red Gulch Road climbs through sage-covered plateaus and badlands toward Alkali Road. WYDOT advises allowing at least an hour for the drive; grades do not exceed seven percent. The road can be bumpy and rutted, and no towns, stores or gas stations interrupt the route between its ends. The northern entrance has a kiosk with historical information and road conditions.

Oil exploration helped improve Red Gulch Road in the late 1950s. Heavy machinery traveled to and from well sites on the Cherry Anticline, but twelve wells failed to yield enough oil for commercial production. The wells were abandoned. Alkali Road had an earlier purpose: completed in 1897, it carried mail across the Big Horn Mountains.

Start at US 14, four miles west of Shell, and follow the byway south toward the Red Gulch Dinosaur Tracksite. Beyond the tracks, red Chugwater walls accompany the climb toward the junction with Alkali Road. At the summit, the Absaroka Mountains are visible across the basin to the west. The byway turns south on Alkali Road and ends north of Hyattville.

moments.title: Red Gulch Dinosaur Tracksite
moments.text: Dinosaur footprints were discovered here in 1997, preserved in limestone near Shell. Before the tracks were found, most scientists thought the whole Big Horn Basin lay beneath the Sundance Sea. The tracks survived as mud hardened, sediment filled the impressions and later erosion uncovered them. Most of the footprints occupy an area called the ballroom. The track-makers remain unidentified: Middle Jurassic dinosaur skeletons are rare in North America, leaving few fossils for comparison. The tracks occupy limestone low in the Sundance Formation; marine fossils in the layer above record a later return of the sea.
moments.notice: Look for dinosaur footprints in the area called the ballroom.

moments.title: Chugwater Formation
moments.text: Iron and oxygen give the Chugwater walls their red color. The sediment accumulated in an inland sea, and the resulting red walls can be seen for miles. Here Red Gulch Road steadily gains elevation through sage-covered plateaus and badlands on its way to Alkali Road. The badlands have intricate erosion patterns and sparse vegetation. Elsewhere along the road, water and wind have shaped steep canyons, caves and table rocks.
moments.notice: Notice the red Chugwater walls and the sparsely vegetated badlands along the climb.

moments.title: Alkali Road
moments.text: The summit junction opens a view west across the Big Horn Basin to the Absaroka Mountains near Cody. Red Gulch Road meets Alkali Road here. Completed in 1897, Alkali Road served as a mail route over the Big Horn Mountains between Big Horn and Hyattville. Mail traveled by wagon, horseback, sled and snowshoes, and crossing the mountain took several long days. The scenic backway follows Alkali Road south; the northern branch climbs toward the Bighorn National Forest. At the southern end, a kiosk describes the backway's historical, archaeological and cultural features, with Hyattville and Manderson nearby.

practical: Red Gulch Dinosaur Tracksite: Travel Wyoming advises driving the backway when open and dry, between May and October. WYDOT warns that even light precipitation can make it muddy and impassable; there are no towns, stores or gas stations along the route. (checked 2026-10-11)
